name: application-controller
intent: Centralise the application-level decisions that advance a stateful interaction: given an event and conversation context, choose the next step, its guard and the domain command to run, then return an abstract view decision so page controllers and views render rather than re-deriving the flow.
problem: Wizard-style interactions and other ordered processes spread navigation decisions across page controllers and views: each screen independently decides what may follow, which permissions or validation outcomes branch the path, and which command to invoke. The same condition is then implemented several times, changes require coordinated edits, and there is no inspectable, testable answer to what happens for a given event and accumulated context.
context: Applies when an interaction has a genuine ordered flow: screens are reached in a meaningful sequence, some transitions are conditional, and the next step depends on state accumulated earlier in the conversation. It is a presentation-boundary pattern independent of view technology, distinct from a Front Controller that dispatches requests, a Page Controller that handles one screen, and an Intercepting Filter that wraps cross-cutting request work. Fowler's caveat still applies: if any screen may be shown in any order there is no flow to centralise. Scope one Application Controller to a related journey or process, not the whole application.
benefits: The flow is written once: step order, conditional branches and entry conditions live in a single artifact instead of being re-derived by every page controller and every view.
Views and page controllers become small and reusable - they render a step and delegate the decision - so a screen can participate in more than one flow without hard-coding what comes next.
Domain work is addressed as commands, so the same unit of work can be triggered from several steps and the domain model stays free of screen references.

The flow becomes an inspectable, testable artifact: it can be driven from events and context alone (no HTTP request, no rendered page), reviewed as one diff, and, when modelled as a state machine, checked for unreachable states and illegal transitions.
Cross-cutting conditions - authentication, authorisation, validation gates, feature toggles - are applied at one choke point, consistently, instead of per screen.
Multi-step conversations can be paused and resumed deliberately: progress is one piece of session state with an owner, a lifetime and a single place to expire or migrate it.
Multiple controllers allow the flow to be scoped to a specific process (checkout, onboarding) without forcing an unrelated part of the application to share the same state machine.
tradeoffs: The controller becomes a change hotspot and readily a god object: it must know every step, every command and every guard, so unrelated features meet in one class and the flow's cohesion decays into 'everything that happens'.
It adds a layer of indirection to every interaction; for two or three screens, or when any screen may be reached in any order, the controller costs more than the duplication it removes.

Flow state must live somewhere between requests (session, cache, client round-trip), bringing serialisation, expiry, versioning and concurrent-replay hazards - two tabs or a double submit can interleave transitions - that a stateless page controller does not have.

The decision rules move away from the screens that used to hold them: a screen's precondition now sits in the controller while the screen sits in the view, so understanding one screen may require reading the controller, and views that keep their own links ('flow drift') silently re-create the duplication.

Declarative flow tables (XML rules, transition tables, configuration) escape the type checker: renames, unreachable states and illegal transitions surface at runtime unless tests or a generator re-establish the check.

Testing requires the controller to be decoupled from the UI machinery; if it reads the HTTP request or the session directly, every flow test needs a request harness and the centralised flow becomes the hardest thing in the application to test.

A single global Application Controller for a large application becomes a bottleneck: unrelated flows are forced together, and any change to one flow risks breaking another that happens to share the same controller.

participants.responsibility: Owns the flow: receives an event (submitted step, chosen action, domain callback) together with the conversation context and decides which domain command to run and which view to show next.
Encapsulates one unit of work against the model - a command object, a transaction-script invocation or a direct domain call - so the controller itself contains no domain logic.
The presentation resource the controller selects for the next step (a page or template id, a view class, a route name), kept abstract so the controller is not bound to a rendering technology.

The rule mapping current state plus event to the next state - a guard predicate, a decision object or a state-machine transition - which keeps entry conditions such as permissions and validation in one place.
Carries the progress and the partial data accumulated across steps (session-scoped, with a defined lifetime and version) so the controller can decide without reconstructing state from the request.

Decouples the controller from specific UI events by publishing application-level events that multiple components can subscribe to independently; the Application Controller publishes rather than calls directly.

use_cases: Checkout and order wizards: cart to address to payment to review to confirmation, with branches for guest versus known buyers and for different payment providers.
Onboarding and registration processes whose step sequence depends on the data already given (company versus private customer, documents required only in some jurisdictions).
Insurance, banking and public-administration form flows where later screens are legally reachable only after earlier ones and every transition must be auditable.
Desktop or rich-client applications with a screen catalog and session state, where the same screens serve several processes and their order is a product decision.
Human-task workflow features (expense approval, ticket triage) driven from a browser, where the next screen depends on the user's role and on the current state of the entity.
Configuration and media wizards in which steps can be revisited out of order but only certain transitions are legal, and progress must survive an interruption.

Client-side single-page application (React, Angular, Vue) wizards and multi-step forms, where a state-machine-based flow manager (XState, Redux-based state machines, dedicated wizard libraries) plays the role of the Application Controller and the accumulated form data is the conversation state.

Microservice choreography sagas where each step of a long-running business transaction is handled by a different service and an orchestrating Application Controller (or saga orchestrator) tracks the overall progress.

Healthcare intake and clinical trial enrollment forms where regulatory compliance requires that certain questions are answered in sequence and changes to responses trigger re-evaluation of downstream eligibility gates.

Document submission workflows (grant applications, permit requests, tax filings) where the sequence of screens depends on prior answers, documents must be uploaded before proceeding, and the entire submission must be resumable after session timeout.

E-commerce returns and refunds processing, where the reason, condition assessment, and resolution options (refund, exchange, store credit) form a conditional branch tree with legal and policy gates at each step.

Loan origination and underwriting flows spanning identity verification, income documentation, credit check, terms selection, and co-borrower addition — where later steps are conditionally revealed based on earlier results.

DevOps and infrastructure provisioning wizards (Kubernetes cluster setup, CI/CD pipeline builders) where each step exposes platform-specific options and the next step's available choices depend on earlier selections.

AWS Step Functions or Azure Logic App-style long-running orchestrations: a server-side Application Controller acts as the saga orchestrator, tracking progress across distributed Lambda/Function steps with compensating transactions on failure.

Multi-tenant SaaS onboarding where the set of configuration steps (branding, billing, team invites, integrations) varies by subscription tier, requiring a conditional flow definition per plan rather than a single linear wizard.

Spring Web Flow checkout and booking flows, where view-state transitions, decision states and flow-scoped data make the reusable sequence an explicit application controller rather than a chain of page redirects.

Jakarta Faces applications using faces-config.xml navigation cases and NavigationHandler, where action outcomes are resolved centrally to the next view while individual backing beans remain page actions.

Oracle ADF bounded task flows, where the ADF Controller's control-flow rules (control-flow-case with to-activity-id, from-action and EL conditions) resolve the next activity centrally and the bounded flow's managed beans and call scope carry the conversation state.

Django formtools SessionWizardView, where WizardView owns the step sequence, condition_dict callables decide which steps are reachable from the accumulated cleaned_data, and session storage holds the conversation - a framework-supplied Application Controller for multi-step forms.

AWS Step Functions state machines as a server-side flow controller: Amazon States Language declares states, Choice branches and Task work, and the service executes the (event, current-state) decision on every step - the transition-table form of the pattern lifted out of the request tier.

Rails applications using inherited ActionController before_action, after_action and around_action callbacks to centralise authentication, authorization or transaction gates around many actions; this is a partial request-lifecycle embodiment, not a substitute for a stateful wizard controller.
avoid_when: Any screen may be reached at any time (dashboards, CRUD admin, content sites): there is no application flow to centralise; use a Front Controller for request dispatch and Page Controllers for screen-specific handling.

The requirement is only one page or endpoint's request handling: a Page Controller should own that screen's input and response, because introducing a cross-screen flow controller adds indirection without removing duplicated transitions.

The requirement is only a cross-cutting before/after concern (authentication, logging, caching, transaction setup): use an Intercepting Filter or framework middleware, which wraps requests but does not own conversation-state transitions.
The interaction is a single page whose state is a handful of UI booleans: a component-level state machine or plain component state suffices, and a server-side controller adds a layer for nothing.
A domain-layer process already owns the transitions (workflow or BPM engine, process manager, saga): the presentation layer should dispatch to it and render its answers, not duplicate its rules.
The sequence is already produced by framework scaffolding (generated CRUD screens) or is a two-step interaction where the duplication the pattern removes does not exist yet.

There is no place to keep conversation state between requests (strictly stateless or serverless request model with no session store) and the steps are short: keep each step independent and idempotent instead.
The application is small enough that a single developer can keep all the navigation logic in their head; introducing a controller adds infrastructure for a problem that does not yet exist.
anti_patterns: 'Controller as god object': the Application Controller accumulates domain rules, persistence and rendering because everything already passes through it, so no flow can change without risking behaviour everywhere.
'Flow drift': views and page controllers keep their own navigation links and redirects, so the controller no longer describes the real flow and the duplication it removed comes back silently.

'Controller in name only': a class called ApplicationController that merely routes URLs or renders one page while real navigation stays inside individual screens; that is a Front Controller or Page Controller, not an Application Controller.

'Implicit flow': encoding the process in redirect chains, hidden form fields, URL paths or filter order instead of a transition decision, so the flow exists only at runtime and can be neither reviewed nor tested.
'Eternal session': conversation state that is never expired or versioned, so stale wizards resume into states the deployed code no longer knows and users get stuck.
'Screen-named states': modelling the machine over template names instead of application situations, so renaming a view breaks the flow and screens that should share a state cannot.

'Static Application Controller': a static class used as a global singleton for navigation, hiding dependencies behind a service-locator anti-pattern and making unit testing impossible without global state.

'Transition-as-if/else chains': encoding flow decisions as scattered if/else blocks inside the controller instead of as a declarative transition table or state machine, so the flow can only be understood by executing the code.

'Step-specific state machine': one monolithic state machine containing every flow in the application, so unrelated teams must coordinate changes to the same artifact and the risk of regressions in one flow from changes in another is maximised.

'Trusting client-side step ids': persisting the current step id in a hidden form field or client-side state without server-side validation, allowing users to skip mandatory steps by tampering with the request.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: flow decisions, domain work and rendering are three responsibilities, not one screen's private business.
Single responsibility and information hiding: a page controller knows its screen, the application controller knows the flow, and neither needs the other's internals.
DRY: one decision point instead of the same navigation condition re-derived in every screen that participates in the process.
Open/closed principle: new steps and commands arrive as new command objects or transitions, not as edits to every screen that might lead there.
Dependency inversion: commands, guards and views are referenced through abstractions or registries, so the flow can be driven from more than one front end.
KISS/YAGNI: centralise only where flow logic genuinely exists; a two-screen interaction does not need a controller.
Explicit over implicit: model the flow as a state machine or transition table rather than encoding it in URL paths, hidden fields or redirect chains.
One controller per flow: scope the Application Controller to a specific process (checkout, onboarding) rather than making one global controller for the entire application.
best_practices: Keep the controller free of UI machinery: pass in an abstract context (progress, user, submitted data) rather than the request or session object, so the flow can be unit-tested without a server.

Return a decision (next view plus command) from the controller instead of rendering inside it; let the caller translate that decision into a response - this composes cleanly with Action-Domain-Responder.
Model the flow explicitly - a transition table, a guard list or a state machine - and keep exactly one canonical representation of it; generated or duplicated copies drift.
Reference views by abstract id and resolve them outside the controller, so the same flow can drive server pages, a rich client or a test double.
Apply guards (authentication, authorisation, validation) at the transition, not in the view, and make them pure so they can be tested as data.
Persist conversation state with a lifetime, a version and an optimistic-concurrency check; expire abandoned flows deliberately and treat a stale step id as an error, not as a silent reset.
Test the flow table exhaustively (every event in every state, including illegal ones) and assert the view chosen for each transition.
Prefer one Application Controller per distinct user journey (checkout wizard, onboarding wizard) rather than a single shared controller; this prevents unrelated flows from coupling to each other.
Combine with the Command pattern and an Event Aggregator: commands handle discrete work, events allow other parts of the UI to react without coupling to the controller directly.
When the flow grows beyond a transition table, graduate to a proper state machine (XState, UML state diagram) that can be simulated, tested with model-checking tools and visualized as a diagram.
Design the conversation state as a versioned snapshot: when a step's data model changes, old sessions can still deserialize via a migration function rather than silently breaking.

Prevent concurrent flow replay: enforce a single active flow per session by validating the current step version or sequence number before applying a transition, so double-submits and multi-tab interactions cannot interleave transitions.

Place guards at transitions rather than inside step handlers: each transition should evaluate preconditions atomically and reject invalid events with a typed error, keeping the guard logic co-located with the flow definition.

Version the flow definition alongside conversation state: when the flow definition evolves (steps added, renamed, reordered), old in-flight conversations must be migratable; treat flow version as part of the session schema.
Expose the flow as a declarative artifact (state chart, transition matrix) separate from the controller class, so it can be reviewed, visualized and model-checked without reading implementation code.

For SPA implementations, prefer libraries with formal state machine semantics (XState, Stately) over ad-hoc boolean flags or useState chains: the controller role is played by the machine, and the resulting flow is inspectable, serializable and testable without a browser.

Use an Event Aggregator to decouple the controller from UI events: the controller publishes navigation decisions, and views or services subscribe independently, preventing bidirectional coupling between the flow and the rendering layer.

Implement explicit timeout handling in the Application Context: when a conversation sits idle past its TTL, return the user to a defined recovery state (e.g., resume or restart) rather than silently dropping them at an arbitrary step.

related_patterns_notes.front-controller: dispatches each request to an entry point, whereas the Application Controller decides the next step within an already identified interaction.
related_patterns_notes.page-controller: handles one screen's request and response, whereas the Application Controller coordinates transitions across several screens.
related_patterns_notes.action-domain-responder: separates request input, domain action and response rendering; the Application Controller supplies the flow decision that chooses the action and next view.
related_patterns_notes.command: encapsulates work for a transition, while the Application Controller selects which command to invoke.
related_patterns_notes.state: carries the current application situation; the Application Controller interprets that state with an event to choose a legal transition.
related_patterns_notes.service-to-worker: delegates a unit of work to a worker, whereas the Application Controller coordinates the user-facing sequence around that work.
related_patterns_notes.context-object: carries conversation state and dependencies through a flow; it is data for the Application Controller, not the component that decides navigation.
related_patterns_notes.intercepting-filter: wraps requests for cross-cutting pre/post processing, whereas the Application Controller owns stateful screen transitions.
related_patterns_notes.event-aggregator: publishes application events to decouple senders and subscribers; the Application Controller may consume or publish them but still owns the flow decision.
related_patterns_notes.workflow: names the broader business process, while the Application Controller is its presentation-boundary coordinator when screens must follow that process.
related_patterns_notes.humble-view: keeps rendering passive and testable; the Application Controller complements it by selecting the next abstract view.
related_patterns_notes.presentation-model: exposes view-ready state and behavior, whereas the Application Controller decides which presentation model or view follows an event.
related_patterns_notes.process-manager: coordinates a long-running domain process across commands and messages; the Application Controller should delegate to it instead of duplicating those domain transitions. coordinates distributed transactions and compensations; an Application Controller coordinates the user's screens and may dispatch to a saga.
related_patterns_notes.mediator: is the general object that directs collaborators, while this pattern narrows that responsibility to application-flow navigation.
related_patterns_notes.state-machine: provides the formal transition model that can implement an Application Controller; the pattern does not require a particular state-machine library.
related_patterns_notes.bpm-engine: executes durable, often human-task business processes; the Application Controller should render and dispatch its decisions rather than become a second BPM engine.
